title: Justice gap: Fair resolution exceeds legal assistance
desc: Defines unmet need broadly through resources, recognition, trust, language and capability rather than a market for cheaper services.

kps.k: The cluster frames access to justice as unmet basic needs at population scale, not simply a market for cheaper legal services.
kps.d: The sources describe housing, safety, health, family and income problems that existing services cannot adequately address. LSC’s 2022 study, based on 2021 survey and intake data, found that 74% of low-income households experienced a civil legal problem and that 92% of substantially impactful personal problems received no or insufficient legal help. These are household-prevalence and problem-level assistance measures, respectively—not percentages of people denied justice. The United States generally provides no entitlement to publicly funded civil counsel, subject to jurisdiction- and case-specific exceptions. Later sources repeatedly cite LSC; those citations do not constitute independent confirmation.

kps.k: A central conceptual dispute concerns whether success means more legal assistance or more lawful and fair resolutions.
kps.d: In Access to What?, Sandefur argues that lawyers form only part of the solution and makes lawful resolution the criterion for expanded access. IAALS and HiiL instead operationalise a broader, respondent-assessed fair-resolution gap across income groups and both civil and criminal problems. Their 2020 online survey of 10,058 people supports an indicative estimate of 120 million problems annually without fair resolution. That extrapolation depends on representativeness and recall assumptions, including dividing four-year reports by three to compensate for forgotten problems. It is not interchangeable with LSC’s low-income civil-assistance measure. These approaches differ in what they measure, rather than directly contradicting one another.

kps.k: Resource shortages constrain legal aid, but the adequacy of funding and lawyer-centred expansion remains contested.
kps.d: LSC’s intake census estimates that organisations provide some help for 51% of eligible problems but no or insufficient help for 71%, approximately 1.4 million annually. The annualisation assumes a typical four-week intake period, and sufficiency includes providers’ expectations rather than only completed outcomes. CRS supplies historical funding context: inflation-adjusted basic field funding per eligible person fell from $7.54 in 2007 to $5.85 in 2016. Institutional recommendations reported in the 2023 legal-aid update call for substantial resources, more legal-services lawyers and broader participation beyond lawyers. Rethinking the Lawyers’ Monopoly argues that even large funding increases would remain inadequate and cites a pro bono requirement exceeding 900 hours per attorney annually. That is a scale argument, not an observed test of expanded funding.

qs.q: LSC’s 2021 Intake Census data indicate that LSC-funded organizations are able to provide legal help for one-half (51%) of the eligible problems low-income individuals bring to them.
qs.a: The Justice Gap: The Unmet Civil Legal Needs of Low-income Americans (2022) · Access to justice · 2022

kps.k: Cost matters, but recognition, trust, language and practical capability also shape whether people seek help.
kps.d: LSC reports that 46% of low-income respondents who did not seek help for at least one problem cited cost; respondents did not think a lawyer could help with 44% of problems and were unsure about another 30%. Sandefur places greater emphasis on people interpreting difficulties as ordinary life problems rather than potential legal claims. AI, UPL, & A2J treats cost’s relative importance as unsettled, contrasting general research with much higher cost concerns among family-court litigants. Access to A.I. Justice adds language and social-resource barriers. These findings concern different populations and settings and do not establish one universal cause. Measures of Justice consequently recommends locating assistance where people already are, rather than relying on self-referral; LSC proposes stronger intake and follow-up support.

kps.k: Need extends beyond poverty, while burdens and access remain unequal.
kps.d: LSC finds substantial-problem assistance gaps of 92% for low-income people, 86% for the middle-income group and 78% for those at or above 400% of the federal poverty level. IAALS and HiiL report broadly similar problem prevalence across incomes but unequal seriousness and resolution, including lower complete-resolution rates for rural residents and several disadvantaged demographic groups. LSC’s 2021 respondents also attributed pandemic-related problems more frequently to low-income circumstances: 33% of low-income adults reported such problems versus 18% of higher-income adults. These are self-reported pandemic links, not causal estimates. The practical implication advanced in the sources is broad access provision combined with targeted attention to especially burdensome problems and underserved groups.

kps.k: More service contacts do not necessarily establish better substantive outcomes.
kps.d: Generative AI and Legal Aid cites evidence favouring tenant representation, including the 2020 Shriver Report’s near-zero defaults among represented tenants and subsequent rental housing for 71% of represented tenants versus 43% without an attorney. These findings concern representation, not AI. In Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice, Rostain and O’Hara distinguish providers’ rationale for brief advice—serving more people with fewer lawyers—from limited evidence of substantive benefits. They cite one study reporting procedural improvements without significant substantive effects, although the supplied passage leaves its qualification incomplete. This is not a direct disagreement about the same intervention: service intensity, dispute type and outcome measure differ. It supports evaluating what assistance accomplishes, not just how many people receive it.

kps.k: AI offers two proposed access pathways, but these passages establish their rationale rather than their effectiveness.
kps.d: The ABA Task Force’s August 2024 report identifies lawyer productivity and direct, understandable legal information and assistance as distinct potential benefits. Generative AI and Legal Aid focuses specifically on augmenting legal-aid organisations. Neither supplied excerpt demonstrates improved AI-assisted outcomes. Legal Tech for Non-Lawyers describes existing tools as mainly informational, referral-based or document-generating. Hagan’s LIST discussion asks whether technology can connect everyday descriptions to legal categories, while her earlier analysis warns that estimated legal need does not measure online help-seeking demand. Thus cheaper or more available tools may address capacity without necessarily overcoming recognition, engagement or resolution barriers.

qs.q: Generative AI has the potential to improve access to justice in two ways: (1) by increasing the efficiency and productivity of legal services and pro bono lawyers, so that they can assist many more people with higher levels of service; and (2) by making accurate, usable, and understandable legal information and assistance easily available to individuals with civil legal problems.
qs.a: ABA Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence — Year 1 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law (August 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: 25 While generative AI has the potential to address these and other problems, the focus of our study is on augmenting the capacity of legal aid organizations to meet the demands of clients.

kps.k: The reform agenda combines service redesign with evidence and sustained implementation, rather than treating pilots as proof of scale.
kps.d: IAALS and HiiL recommend user-centred services integrated with social, health and educational interventions, alongside enabling regulation and prevention. Utah lists self-help, licensed paralegal practitioners, form reform and online dispute resolution, but the supplied material does not evaluate their effects. Hagan’s Paths Toward Access to Justice at Scale argues that pilots often expire with initial funding and that implicit theories of change impede wider implementation; she presents this as one possible explanation, not a tested sole cause. Better longitudinal and linked data could clarify which services work for whom. Measurement must also capture people outside courts and completed intake, and must not turn LSC’s differently designed 2017 and 2022 studies into a precise worsening trend.

qs.q: To date, the Supreme Court, along with the Judicial Council  and the Utah Bar Association, have worked ceaselessly to improve  access to justice through many initiatives: the Utah Courts Self-Help  Center, the Licensed Paralegal Practitioner Program, form reform, and  the Online Dispute Resolution Program, to name but a few.

vlens.an: The curated academia-and-research sources collectively accept the proposition that the justice gap is broader than a market shortage of affordable lawyers and should be understood through people’s ability to obtain lawful or fair resolution. Their common reasons are that unmet problems affect basic needs at population scale; cost and legal-aid capacity are important but incomplete explanations; many people do not recognise problems as legal or lack knowledge, confidence, trust, language access and practical capability; and additional service contacts or technological tools cannot be presumed to improve substantive outcomes. The voice materially develops the proposition through concrete research and design priorities: technology-assisted issue recognition, assistance situated where problems arise, outcome-focused and longitudinal evaluation, wider measurement that includes omitted populations and problem categories, and explicit theories of change for scaling reforms. Material internal variation concerns emphasis rather than opposition. Sandefur supplies the clearest fair-resolution criterion; Hagan and related work focus on recognition, service design and implementation; legal-aid and AI studies remain more lawyer-capacity-centred and describe AI benefits as potential; some sources stress affordability, funding or deregulation; and two excerpts are too limited to establish a position. The evidence also cautions that representation can improve outcomes in some settings while brief advice and existing legal technologies may offer limited or unproven substantive benefits. This assessment applies only to the curated sources and does not imply that it represents academia or research generally.

vlens.an: These curated access-to-justice and civil-society sources accept the proposition that the justice gap concerns people’s ability to resolve consequential problems, not merely demand for cheaper legal services, and materially develop it through complementary empirical measures. Both connect unmet need to basic matters such as housing, family, health, safety and livelihoods, and both identify barriers beyond price, including uncertainty about whether lawyers can help, limited confidence, practical intake difficulties and inadequate service capacity. They also support evaluating resolution or sufficiency rather than counting service contacts alone. Material variation lies in scope and outcome definition: IAALS and HiiL measure a respondent-assessed fair-resolution gap across income groups and both civil and criminal problems, whereas LSC measures unmet civil legal assistance among low-income Americans and capacity constraints within LSC-funded organisations. Accordingly, the former more directly advances the proposition that fair resolution exceeds legal assistance, while the latter supports it indirectly from an assistance- and resource-centred framework. Their estimates also require different cautions: IAALS and HiiL’s national extrapolation is explicitly indicative and assumption-dependent, while LSC’s survey and intake measures concern reported help and provider capacity rather than independently verified substantive outcomes. These positions describe only the supplied sources, not access-to-justice or civil-society professionals generally.

vlens.an: The selected regulators, courts and professional bodies generally support the proposition’s broad diagnosis: unmet civil legal need is population-scale, affects basic necessities, and cannot be reduced simply to demand for cheaper legal services. The Utah source expressly defines access to justice as meaningful access to solutions encompassing information, advice, resources and courts, while the ABA Task Force links the gap to shelter, safety, family stability and subsistence. Material variation concerns the solution and outcome criteria. The ABA report concentrates on potential AI-enabled lawyer productivity and direct assistance but does not show that these pathways produce fair resolutions. Utah lists institutional reforms without evaluating their effects. CRS provides strong historical evidence of shortages, underfunding and assistance beyond representation, but does not address recognition, trust, language, capability or fair resolution directly. Thus this professional voice supports the proposition’s scale and breadth more clearly than its specific fair-resolution framework.

qs.q: The matters in which Americans lack access to legal representation often involve the most basic of human needs: shelter (protection against unlawful evictions and foreclosures); personal safety (protection orders against abusers); family stability (child custody, child support, guardianships, and adoptions); and financial subsistence (job security, wage theft, and access to benefits programs).
qs.a: ABA Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence — Year 1 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law (August 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an: The pre-2015 source supports the proposition’s core diagnosis that the justice gap is a large-scale failure of access rather than merely a demand for marginally cheaper legal services. It documents widespread nonrepresentation and non-engagement with the justice system, links these conditions to legal fees, and shows that legal aid, public-interest and other subsidized services account for only a small fraction of legal effort. Its support is narrower than the completed synthesis: the source primarily frames the gap through affordability and inadequate provider capacity, without developing the later emphasis on fair resolution, legal-problem recognition, trust, language, practical capability or substantive outcomes. It therefore supplies an important foundation for the proposition but not its full multidimensional account. Because this time period contains only one curated source, no cross-source prevalence or material internal variation can be inferred.

qs.q: Only routine legal work seems afford­ able: $100 for a simple will, $350 for an uncontested divorce, $425 for an individual bankruptcy.23     Free or subsidized services - legal aid, public interest, pro bona, and publicly provided legal services - account for a tiny fraction of legal effort.
qs.a: The Price of Law: How the Market for Lawyers Distorts the Justice System · Academia · 2000

elens.an: The curated 2015–2022 sources collectively accept the proposition that the justice gap cannot be reduced to the price or availability of lawyers, and materially develop it in several ways. Sandefur reframes the objective as lawful resolution rather than lawyer access; IAALS and HiiL operationalise a broader, respondent-assessed fair-resolution gap spanning income groups and both civil and criminal problems; and other sources identify recognition, trust, language, practical capability and provider capacity as distinct barriers. The period also adds empirical scale and distributional evidence, especially through the 2021 IAALS/HiiL survey and LSC’s 2021 survey and intake census, while carefully distinguishing fair-resolution measures from legal-assistance measures. Material internal variation remains: LSC and several historical or administrative accounts principally measure unmet assistance and resource shortages, so they support only part of the broader proposition; CRS and A Rule of Persons, Not Machines do not clearly adopt the outcome-focused framing. Legal Tech for Non-Lawyers extends the scope to categories often omitted from civil surveys and cautions that available tools mainly provide information, referrals or documents, rather than demonstrated fair resolution. Technology optimism within the period is therefore prospective rather than evidence that automation improves outcomes.

elens.an: The 2023–2024 sources collectively accept the proposition that the justice gap is a population-scale problem involving basic needs and barriers beyond price or service supply. Across this curated set, recurring reasons include severe legal-aid capacity constraints, the absence of a general right to civil counsel, courts designed around represented users, and obstacles involving problem recognition, confidence, capability, trust, geography and emotional inhibition. The period materially develops the proposition by distinguishing underlying legal need from demand for online help, questioning whether brief advice or additional service contacts improve substantive outcomes, and calling for longitudinal, outcome-focused evidence. There is meaningful internal variation: the legal-aid update emphasises resources and participation beyond lawyers; the ABA report frames generative AI as a potential route to lawyer productivity and direct assistance but does not establish effectiveness; Measures of Justice recommends placing help where people encounter problems rather than relying on self-referral; and Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice most clearly extends the cluster toward evaluation of fair outcomes. The bibliographic-only excerpt provides no attributable position. These selected sources should not be treated as representative of all commentary from the period.

The 2025 sources accept the proposition that the justice gap is population-scale and cannot be reduced to demand for cheaper lawyers. They commonly point to extensive unmet civil legal need, constrained legal-aid capacity and barriers extending beyond price, including awareness, procedural access, language and confidence that the legal system can help. Collectively, they materially develop the proposition in two ways: one source makes visible society-wide standards of fairness an objective alongside fair individual outcomes, while others explore generative AI or broader regulatory change as possible capacity responses. Material variation remains. Some sources retain a lawyer-capacity emphasis, stressing representation benefits and shortages of attorneys; another explicitly argues that access need not depend on lawyers or courts; and the lawyers’ monopoly source argues that even very large increases in legal-aid funding or pro bono work would be insufficient. The AI-oriented sources describe potential pathways rather than evidence of adoption at scale or improved AI-assisted outcomes. These curated sources therefore build on the proposition conceptually and institutionally, but do not establish that proposed technology or service reforms work at scale.

The 2026 sources accept the cluster’s principal proposition that the justice gap is broader than the availability or price of legal assistance, and they materially extend its implementation agenda. Both focus on mechanisms that can prevent unmet need from becoming fair resolution: one addresses recognition and language by asking whether technology can translate people’s everyday descriptions into legal categories; the other addresses durability and scale by arguing that reform initiatives need intentional, explicit theories of change. Their common rationale is that neither existing resources nor isolated interventions are sufficient if people cannot identify relevant legal dimensions, locate suitable help, or if promising programmes fail to spread and persist. The internal variation is mainly one of level and evidentiary status. The LIST source concentrates on user-facing issue spotting and frames technology as a design question, without demonstrating effectiveness or fairer outcomes. The scaling paper concentrates on field-level strategy and identifies absent theories of change as one underexamined explanation, not a tested sole cause. Thus, these curated sources develop complementary recognition and implementation dimensions of the proposition rather than opposing its fair-resolution framing.
